To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the circadian rhythms in temperature and wake of rats exposed to continuous illumination eventually damped out and that ultradian variations in temperature and wake persisted when circadian rhythms were absent.
the circadian rhythm in temperature is stronger and longer-lasting than the circadian wake rhythm, and that the ultradian wake rhythm may be the cause of the ultradian temperature rhythm.
In the rat, circadian rhythms of wake and temperature can free-run in parallel, and eventually damp out in the absence of external time cues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
circadian and ultradian rhythms in temperature and wakefulness of rats under continuous illumination.
the circadian and ultradian rhythms of body temperature and wake in the rat.
the properties of the biological clock, which controls the temperature and sleep/wake cycles in the rat, under continuous illumination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a circadian rhythm of core temperature is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the circadian rhythm in wakefulness.
the circadian rhythms in temperature and wake were controlled by a single circadian oscillator, and that the ultradian variations were controlled by a separate oscillator.
circadian rhythms of both temperature and wake can be controlled by a single circadian oscillator, and that this oscillator is not dependent upon the circadian rhythm in sleep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the circadian rhythm is not a necessary condition for the ultradian rhythm.
the circadian rhythms are controlled by one or more circadian oscillators which are sensitive to light.

the circadian rhythm in the rat is controlled by a single, temperature-compensated oscillator, and that the ultradian variations in temperature and wake are controlled by separate, non-temperature-compensated oscillators, which are coupled to the circadian oscillator.
The main takeaway from our work is that
circadian rhythms can be lost in continuous illumination, and that this loss is not a result of the animal's being awake.
continuous light can induce circadian arrhythmy, and that the circadian and ultradian rhythms of wake are dissociable from those of temperature.
circadian and ultradian rhythms are not independent of each other.
